chapters.title: An easy button, a harder problem
chapters.text: Booking an appointment looks like a simple click. But two people may request the same doctor and time. A reliable system must make one correct decision, even when both screens looked available.

chapters.title: Check authority before writing
chapters.text: CareIndex checks the request origin and session first. Staff need the right permission. A patient account is tied to its own fictional profile, so changing a browser field cannot book for an unrelated patient.

chapters.title: Put the check inside the transaction
chapters.text: The booking path begins an immediate SQLite transaction before checking availability. SQLite serialises writers. This prevents two independent check-then-write sequences from both treating the same slot as free.

chapters.title: Keep the invariant in the database
chapters.text: A partial unique index allows only one scheduled booking for a doctor, date, and time. The application also checks working hours and existing reservations. The database rule remains a final protection.

chapters.title: Commit the complete change
chapters.text: The appointment and its invoice are created inside the same transaction. Both commit together. If something fails, the transaction rolls back. A competing request receives a controlled conflict instead of a second reservation.

chapters.title: Understand what the demo proves
chapters.text: The engineering lab explains database behaviour and separate algorithms, including A V L rotations. It does not claim that a teaching tree replaces SQLite indexing. All patients are fictional, and payments are simulated.
